title: The son who asked why
hook: Devavrata asks his grieving father why, hears half an answer, and quietly finds the rest: pitru devo bhava
carry: pitru devo bhava: honor your father as god

segments.voice: Yesterday: a fisherman's condition, and a king who wanted her but wouldn't give his son's crown away. Kama is honored, but dharma comes first.
screen: `KAMA IS HONORED, BUT DHARMA COMES FIRST.`

segments.voice: Devavrata, the heir, has watched his father grow quiet and pale, sitting lost in thought, and he can't find a reason for it anywhere. The kingdom is at peace, and nothing is missing that he can see. So the son does something that takes a little nerve with a king. He stands before him and asks straight out: everything in the kingdom is going well, so why are you grieving? And Shantanu answers him. Just not completely.
screen: `HIS FATHER HAS GONE QUIET.` → `THE KINGDOM IS AT PEACE.` → `WHY ARE YOU GRIEVING?`

segments.voice: Here is Shantanu's answer, in the text's sense. You are my only son, and the wise say a man with one son is like a man with none. You're a warrior, always among weapons. If you fell in battle, what would become of our line? Every word of it is something the king could mean. But it isn't the whole reason he's grieving, and the text lets us see that. He can't say: I want a woman whose father demands your crown. Devavrata doesn't argue. He goes to someone who would know, an old minister devoted to his father, and asks. And the old man tells him: the fisherman's daughter by the Yamuna, and her father's condition. Now notice what the son doesn't do. He doesn't confront his father, or sulk about a crown he might lose. He starts to think about what he can do for him. Hindu tradition holds Bhishma up for exactly this. The Taittiriya Upanishad gives students lines to carry when they leave their teacher's house. One is for the mother, and the next is pitru devo bhava: let your father be like God to you. Many teachers read it this way: not that a father is always right, but that a parent's well-being is sacred, worth your time, your attention, even your own sacrifice. That's seva, loving service, and it's why in many Hindu homes grown children care for aging parents, touch their feet, and keep them close. Devavrata hears a half answer, and instead of feeling shut out, he goes looking for what his father couldn't say.
screen: `ONE SON IS LIKE NO SON.` · `HE ASKS THE OLD MINISTER.` · `HE THINKS OF WHAT HE CAN DO.` · `PITRU DEVO BHAVA.` · then, large: `HONOR YOUR FATHER AS GOD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a parent or elder who has cared for you, living or gone. If it's your way, picture yourself touching their feet, the way many Hindus greet parents and elders, and receiving their blessing. Breathe in their care for you; breathe out one small thing you could do for them this week: a call, a cup of chai, an hour of listening. If no parent comes to mind, hold any elder who has been family to you.
Bhishma's vow. Before the vow, a son who hears his father's half answer, and goes to find the rest.
Your line: pitru devo bhava, honor your father as God. Next, a prince at a fisherman's door. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 711 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A VOW BEFORE THE ELDERS.`

howItsDone: Many Hindus touch the feet of parents and elders to receive their blessing, and caring for aging parents is treated as a child's sacred duty; retellings hold Bhishma up as an example of it.

original.note: Sanskrit pitṛdevo bhava, let your father be like God to you: from the Taittiriya Upanishad (1.11).
